records.sourceFile: Structural brain differences in professional Australian rules footballers following mild traumatic brain injury - When head size matters.pdf

paper.citation: Lee JM, Pardoe HR, Parker DM, Pedersen M, Makdissi M, Abbott DF, et al. Structural brain differences in professional Australian rules footballers following mild traumatic brain injury: When head size matters. Front Neurol. 2026;17:1701097.
paper.abstract: Quantified subcortical and cortical structural MRI differences between 31 recently concussed professional Australian rules footballers and 37 healthy non-athlete controls. Footballers had lower proportional hippocampal and amygdala volumes and reduced cortical thickness, but the volumetric findings depended on the intracranial volume estimation method used for normalization.
paper.tldr: Recently concussed professional footballers had smaller hippocampal volumes than non-athlete controls, but the result depends on how head size is estimated. It is a useful cross-sectional signal, not a diagnostic or return-to-play marker.
paper.methods: Retrospective case-control study of 31 professional male footballers scanned within 3 months of a suspected concussion (acute group 17, sub-acute group 14) and 37 healthy male controls. T1-weighted 3 T MRI was processed with FreeSurfer recon-all, and hippocampal and amygdala volumes were normalized to estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV). Vertex-wise cortical thickness and a subset of 12 players with follow-up scans were also analyzed, and two other intracranial volume estimates were compared as an exploratory step.
paper.findings: Players had lower proportional bilateral hippocampal and amygdala volumes than controls at uncorrected p < 0.05, with the bilateral hippocampal differences remaining significant after Bonferroni correction. Players had a cluster of lower right lateral orbitofrontal cortical thickness (peak p = 0.013, exploratory). Players had larger eTIV than controls (p < 0.001). When normalized to segmentation-based total intracranial volume or supratentorial volume, only the right hippocampus differed. In 12 players with follow-up scans, no subcortical volume changed after correction, and a right hippocampal reduction (p = 0.042) did not survive correction. In an exploratory analysis of 25 players, smaller left hippocampal volume correlated with poorer CogSport learning scores (r = 0.44, p = 0.030).
paper.limitations: The cohort is male and all players were professionals, and controls were non-athletes, so sport exposure, head size and injury history are confounded. Prior concussion history was not known. Most ROI results are uncorrected, and the choice of intracranial volume method changed which findings held. The longitudinal sample was small, the cognitive correlations were exploratory, and two scanner models were used.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff interpreting hippocampal or amygdala volume results after concussion should check how intracranial volume was normalized, and should not treat a single MRI volume as evidence of injury or of a future problem. Clinical use needs a larger study with athlete controls and pre-injury baselines.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The study does not measure sport performance. Its only performance-adjacent finding is an exploratory link between smaller left hippocampal volume and poorer learning scores in a subset of players, which is not a basis for selection or training decisions.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study does not link MRI volumes to return-to-play timing, and it cannot be used to clear or hold a player. Most scans were taken within weeks of injury, and no recovery outcome was tied to the volume measures.

records.sourceFile: Subtypes of sport-related concussion - A systematic review and meta-cluster analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Langdon S, Königs M, Adang EAM, Goedhart E, Oosterlaan J. Subtypes of Sport-Related Concussion: a Systematic Review and Meta-cluster Analysis. Sports Med. 2020.
paper.abstract: The authors systematically reviewed 22 studies of sport-related concussion symptom clusters and their links to clinical outcome, aggregating the cluster findings with multiple correspondence analysis. They identified five symptom clusters, with the migraine cluster most often reported and most strongly linked to outcome.
paper.tldr: Concussion symptoms appear to group into about five clusters, and the migraine-type cluster is the one most closely tied to longer recovery. Clinicians may use these groupings to think about symptom profiles, but treatment decisions based on them still need testing.
paper.methods: Systematic review following MOOSE guidance, searching four databases from 1946 to December 2018 for studies that identified symptom clusters or linked clusters to outcomes after sport-related concussion. Two reviewers screened and extracted data, and risk of bias was assessed with an adapted Cochrane tool. Reported clusters were pooled with multiple correspondence analysis, and cluster-outcome links were summarised with effect sizes where available.
paper.findings: Of 22 included studies (5,592 athletes), six found symptom clusters and 19 linked clusters to outcomes. The meta-analysis identified a migraine cluster (headache, light and noise sensitivity, nausea), a cognitive-emotional cluster, a sleep-emotional cluster, a neurological cluster (blurred vision, vomiting, neck pain) and an undefined feelings cluster. Migraine-type clusters were most frequently reported (24%) and linked to prolonged symptom duration and cognitive, balance and oculomotor deficits, with the largest effect sizes. The undefined feelings cluster was not linked to any outcome.
paper.limitations: Most included studies had methodological limitations, and only 13.6% used exploratory data-driven clustering. Clusters were pooled from published reports rather than individual data, and the athletes were mostly adolescents. The authors note that only five included studies adjusted for covariates such as age, sex and time since injury, and all studies assessed symptoms within about the first month after injury. Whether particular clusters relate to specific functional impairments remains unclear.
paper.practicalImplications: Record each athlete's symptom profile after concussion, paying particular attention to headache, light and noise sensitivity, cognitive, sleep and emotional symptoms, since clusters built from these were most often linked to prolonged recovery. Use the profile to guide assessment of headache, neurocognitive, emotional, neurological and sleep function, as the authors recommend, rather than assuming one pathway fits all athletes.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: This review does not address training or performance directly. Its relevance is to recognising concussion profiles and to communicating with athletes about symptom patterns that predict a slower return to training.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Symptom clusters, especially the migraine-type cluster, were linked to prolonged recovery and symptom duration, so they may help flag athletes who need a longer, more cautious return. The review does not show that cluster-based management shortens return to sport, and it cannot set return-to-play timelines.
